Kosala
------------------------------------------
According to the historians, there were two ancient kingdoms by this name. The first was the kingdom ruled over by दशरथ with its capital at अयोध्या on the bank of the river सरयू. The second was the kingdom of Bhānumanta whose daughter कौसल्या had been married to दशरथ as his first wife and chief queen.
In later literature, the former has been known as Uttara-कोसल and the latter as Dakṣiṇa-कोसल.
When राम abdicated his kingdom, he gave the former to लव and the latter to कुश (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa, ch. 107). लव moved the capital to Śrāvasti and कुश established a new city named after him, as Kuśāvatī. अयोध्या was abandoned as the capital.
The Uttara कोसल corresponds roughly to the modern Oudh and the boundaries probably extended up to the hills of Nepal. The ancient अयोध्या has been identified with the twin towns of अयोध्या and Fyzabad in Uttar Pradesh.
The Dakṣiṇa कोसल perhaps extended up to the region of Raipur, Sambal-pur and Bilaspur in Madhya Pradesh.
Sometimes, the word कोसल has been used to indicate a people (vide Raghuvaṁśa 4.77-78).

kośa
(‘that which encloses’)
------------------------------------------
This word is used in two senses. In Vedānta, it indicates the पञ्चकोशस् (five sheaths) that envelop the जीव or the indi-vidual सोउल्. In political science it indicates the treasury of the king.
See PAÑCAKOŚAS and RĀJYĀṄGAS for details.
